name: TrueNAS
summary: Operating system and unified network storage platform (NAS/SAN) developed by iXsystems, powered by the transactional OpenZFS file system and structured around the CORE (FreeBSD) and SCALE (Debian GNU/Linux with Docker and KVM) editions.
license: Open Source (2-Clause BSD licence for the FreeNAS/CORE core, GPL components for the Linux environment of SCALE) with enterprise support options

content.introduction: TrueNAS is a specialised operating system and a unified network storage platform (NAS/SAN) developed by the American company iXsystems. Designed to guarantee absolute data integrity and to simplify file sharing in enterprises and at home, TrueNAS brings together the advanced features of the OpenZFS file system within an environment administered through a web interface, available as free software or integrated into dedicated hardware appliances.
content.what_is_it: Historically derived from the open-source FreeNAS project created in 2005 on a FreeBSD foundation, the system was taken over by iXsystems in 2009 then unified under the TrueNAS brand in 2020. The platform offers two complementary variants: TrueNAS CORE, relying on FreeBSD for pure storage-centred deployments with jails and bhyve, and TrueNAS SCALE, resting on Debian GNU/Linux with a Linux 6.x kernel. TrueNAS SCALE is the flagship of the range, bringing KVM virtualisation, Docker containers and extended clustered storage features.
content.openzfs_architecture_and_data_integrity: The central technological asset of TrueNAS is its native and far-reaching integration of OpenZFS, a 128-bit file system and transactional logical volume manager using copy-on-write. OpenZFS aggregates physical media into storage pools (zpools) divided into virtual devices (vdevs) configurable in mirror, RAIDZ1, RAIDZ2, RAIDZ3 or dRAID. Every data and metadata block is protected by a cryptographic checksum (Fletcher4, SHA-256), allowing automatic detection and correction of silent corruption during scrub cycles. The platform also manages instant snapshots, secure asynchronous replication (`zfs send/receive`), native encryption of datasets and fast deduplication.
content.unified_storage_protocols_and_networking: TrueNAS delivers a unified storage architecture covering file-mode, block-mode and object-mode needs. For network file sharing, it embeds Samba (SMB 2/3) with full support for Windows access control lists (NFSv4 ACLs ported by iXsystems to Linux), NFS (v3, v4.1, v4.2 with multi-stream nconnect acceleration), as well as WebDAV. For block-mode SAN storage, it offers an optimised iSCSI target (SCST under Linux, CTL under FreeBSD) with high performance for remote hypervisors. It also includes Amazon S3-compatible object compatibility (through MinIO) and synchronisation to cloud providers through rclone.
content.application_ecosystem_and_docker_transit: In its modern versions (notably TrueNAS SCALE 24.10 'Electric Eel'), iXsystems has evolved its application architecture by abandoning the complexity of the Kubernetes engine (k3s/Helm) in favour of native integration of Docker Engine and Docker Compose. This major transition allows users to deploy containerised applications directly from the official catalogue or by writing standard `docker-compose.yml` files, while retaining the ability to create complete isolated virtual machines under the KVM hypervisor.
content.administration_webui_and_middleware: System administration takes place through a modern Angular web interface, providing interactive dashboards for real-time supervision of disk status, S.M.A.R.T. health status, hardware temperatures and ZFS memory cache usage (ARC - Adaptive Replacement Cache). All platform functions are controllable through a complete RESTful and WebSocket API served by the TrueNAS middleware, easing automation. TrueNAS Enterprise professional appliances also offer active-passive hardware high availability with no service interruption (dual-controller HA failover).
content.historique_et_transition_du_socle_freebs: The lineage of the platform can be read in its version numbers as much as in its migration documentation. Versions built on FreeBSD stop at the 13.0 and 13.3 branches, and the migration documentation only connects them with the Linux line after an update to their latest maintenance revision. The move to a Linux foundation begins with the 22.12 branch; it can be done by a clean installation from the ISO image of the target version, or through the update train selector from the FreeBSD system to the 24.04 branch (Dragonfish) then, branch by branch, up to the current version. The documentation specifies that the migration does not preserve the application configuration and that it assumes a prior backup of the system configuration file, re-injected after installation. Enterprise systems, for their part, are delivered already installed, and the documentation asks HA customers not to reinstall their two controllers themselves.
content.cycle_de_versions_et_profils_de_mise_a_j: Two numbering regimes coexist. The versions published up to the 25.x series follow the AA.MM scheme (24.10 Electric Eel, 25.04 Fangtooth, 25.10 Goldeye), with four-field maintenance revisions: 24.10.2.4 dated 7 August 2025 and 25.04.2.6 dated 30 October 2025. From TrueNAS 27, the documentation announces an annual pace and an `AA.MINOR.PATCH` format, the major number repeating the stable publication year. On top of that cadence come four update profiles selectable in the Update screen: Developer, Early Adopter, General and Mission Critical. A community system starts from the highest profile available for its version; an Enterprise system has access only to General and Mission Critical, and the Mission Critical profile is the one applied on delivery. The progression rule requires going through the latest maintenance revision of the current branch before changing major branch.
content.catalogue_dapplications_et_depots_logiqu: TrueNAS does not expose a general-purpose package manager to the administrator: application software arrives through a catalogue of containerised applications, described in the documentation as the mechanism for installing and managing applications. The catalogue is published on apps.truenas.com and updated daily; it also defines the support levels associated with applications. The system runs Docker Engine and accepts Compose files, which allows installing a catalogue application or a custom application described by its own file. Version 25.04 adds two elements distinct from the catalogue: the selection of an IP address per application during deployment, and an experimental mechanism of LXC system containers, reserved for community testing. The system software itself does not update through a package repository: the Update screen queries the project's update server or accepts a locally uploaded file.
content.installation_et_verification_des_images: Installation starts from an ISO image published on the project site, to be written to a bootable medium. The iXsystems security team signs these images, and the documentation describes two independent checks before writing: verification of the OpenPGP signature of the `.iso.gpg` or `.iso.sig` file with `gpg --verify` after importing the public key, and verification of the SHA-256 fingerprint provided next to the image. Both can be carried out on the same image, the signature attesting the origin and the fingerprint the integrity of the transfer. What follows is identical on physical hardware and on a virtual machine: boot from the medium, installation, then initial network configuration through the console menu before the first connection to the web interface. A migration from FreeBSD additionally requires updating the source branch to its latest maintenance revision before starting the installation.
advantages: Maximum data protection and integrity thanks to the transactional OpenZFS file system and automatic error correction (self-healing).
Complete unified support for industrial storage protocols: SMB with native Windows ACLs, NFS with nconnect, iSCSI, S3 and WebDAV.
Transition to native Docker Engine and Docker Compose in TrueNAS SCALE radically simplifying the deployment of containerised applications.
Professional backup and disaster recovery capabilities through scheduled ZFS snapshots, lightweight clones and remote replication.
Ergonomic and responsive web interface accompanied by an exhaustive RESTful/WebSocket API for infrastructure automation.
Availability as free software for any x86-64 hardware and as certified hardware appliances for enterprises.
disadvantages: Demanding hardware requirements for OpenZFS, requiring a large amount of RAM (minimum recommendation of 8 to 16 GB of RAM) and preferably ECC memory.
Historical rigidity in modifying the topology of zpools after the fact (extending a RAIDZ vdev disk by disk remaining a recent OpenZFS feature).
The two variants (CORE under FreeBSD and SCALE under Linux) present differences in features and drivers that may require a considered migration.
Continuous energy and thermal consumption inherent to multi-bay storage servers and multi-disk RAID configurations.
Native real-time block deduplication requires substantial processor and memory resources at the risk of degrading I/O throughput.
who_is_it_for: Enterprises, institutions and research centres looking for a centralised, secure and sovereign storage solution for their critical volumes.
System administrators deploying SAN arrays or reliable backup repositories for VMware, Proxmox or Hyper-V hypervisor clusters.
Content creators, post-production studios and agencies handling terabytes of video data requiring high throughput and multi-user SMB/NFS sharing.
Advanced users and home server enthusiasts (homelab) wanting to host their personal data and containerised services under Docker.
who_is_it_not_for: Beginner users looking for a consumer-ready file sharing box without prior knowledge of storage and RAID redundancy.
IT infrastructures constrained by old or undersized hardware with less than 4 to 8 GB of RAM.
Desktop workstations or personal laptops (TrueNAS being a dedicated server system offering no local graphical environment).
Deployments on 32-bit hardware architectures or consumer ARM architectures not officially supported.
content.verdict: TrueNAS is an open-source unified network storage (NAS/SAN) platform built around the OpenZFS file system. It provides built-in file sharing (SMB, NFS, iSCSI), encrypted data replication and RAIDZ volume management services through a web administration interface. With the transition to TrueNAS SCALE based on a Debian Linux kernel and the integration of application containers, the solution suits enterprise storage infrastructures as well as home virtualisation and backup servers.

relations.name: FreeBSD
relations.note: Free Unix operating system forming the historical foundation of the FreeNAS project and of the TrueNAS CORE edition.

relations.name: Debian
relations.note: Linux distribution serving as the foundation for the modern TrueNAS SCALE edition (Linux kernel and Debian user space).

relations.name: Proxmox VE
relations.note: Enterprise hypervisor and virtualisation platform frequently interfaced with TrueNAS for clustered shared storage.

relations.name: OpenMediaVault
relations.note: Lightweight NAS distribution based on Debian, oriented towards more modest hardware architectures.
